questions.text: What is a microtask in the event loop?
options: A job from the microtask queue: Promise.then, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver
Any setTimeout call
A browser paint frame
Synchronous code still on the stack

questions.text: setTimeout(fn, 0) runs before Promise.resolve().then(fn).
What is the event loop?
questions.answer: The mechanism that pulls jobs from queues onto the call stack when the stack is empty. It drains the microtask queue first, then takes one macrotask (timer, I/O), then drains microtasks again.

questions.text: After synchronous code, in what order does the event loop run work?
options: All microtasks, then one macrotask
One macrotask, then all microtasks
Microtasks and macrotasks interleaved by enqueue time
Only macrotasks; microtasks wait for the next tick

questions.text: queueMicrotask puts the callback on the microtask queue.
How is a macrotask different from a microtask?
questions.answer: A macrotask (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O) is one turn of the “big” loop: after it finishes, the event loop drains every microtask. Microtasks (Promise.then, queueMicrotask) have higher priority and run back-to-back until that queue is empty.

What runs before either event-loop queue?
options: Synchronous code on the current call stack
The earliest setTimeout callback

options: Onto the call stack immediately, before the next line
On the macrotask (timer) queue

questions.text: A setTimeout callback can start before the current synchronous function returns.
Two setTimeout(fn, 0) calls made one after another from synchronous code keep their queue order.
A Promise.then callback runs before the next line after .then(...).
While the call stack is not empty, the event loop does not take a task from a queue.
queueMicrotask and Promise.then share one microtask queue.
setTimeout(fn, 0) calls fn synchronously: zero means “no queue”.
While the line after setTimeout(fn, 0) is running, fn is still waiting in a queue.
With no timers and no promises, the event loop still pauses between two console.log calls.
If the executor calls resolve immediately, the then callback still waits until the current synchronous code finishes.
A microtask can start in the middle of a synchronous function, before its return.
Why doesn’t setTimeout(fn, 0) run immediately?
questions.answer: Zero is a timer delay, not “run now”. The callback joins the macrotask queue and starts only after the stack is empty and that queue is reached. Synchronous code and microtasks finish first.

questions.text: What is the call stack for in this model?
questions.answer: It runs the current synchronous code. While it is not empty, the event loop does not pull a task from a queue.

questions.text: Which queue does a Promise.then callback join?
questions.answer: The microtask queue. It runs after the current synchronous code and before macrotasks.

questions.text: How is a new Promise executor different from a then callback?
questions.answer: The executor is called immediately, synchronously. then is always deferred to the microtask queue, even when the promise is already fulfilled.

questions.text: Name two sources of macrotasks.
questions.answer: Timers (setTimeout and setInterval) and I/O: network, files, input events. They are turns of the outer loop, and microtasks are drained between them.

questions.text: Why doesn’t a 0 ms delay put a timer ahead of a synchronous console.log?
questions.answer: A timer does not cut into the current stack. Zero means “queue it as soon as possible”, not “run it before the next line”.

questions.text: The stack is empty and a microtask is already queued. What happens next?
questions.answer: The event loop runs microtasks until that queue is empty, and only then takes one macrotask.

questions.text: Can a microtask start before the current function returns?
questions.answer: No. The function reaches return and the stack unwinds first. Microtasks run after that.

questions.text: In what order do two setTimeout(0) callbacks run if they were queued one after another?
questions.answer: In queue order. The first callback runs to completion, then the second starts. Their lines are not interleaved.

questions.text: Why are microtasks a separate queue instead of being mixed with timers?
questions.answer: So promise reactions can run as a batch right after the current code, without waiting for the next timer. Otherwise then would lose to any setTimeout(0).
